title: Clean on the outside (Luke 11:37–54)
hook: he eats with Pharisees and challenges religion that's all surface

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lamp of the eye, and a single, generous eye that fills the whole body with light. Your line was keep the light in. Did you look at someone again, on purpose? Day five hundred forty-six.

A Pharisee invites Jesus to dinner. That alone is worth noticing: Luke shows him at Pharisees' tables more than once, and it means they took him seriously as a teacher. The Pharisees were a devoted movement who wanted holiness to reach ordinary life, right down to meals and dishes and hands. So when the guest sits straight down without the ritual washing, the host is startled. The King James Bible says he "marvelled that he had not first washed before dinner." And Jesus, at someone else's table, answers the look on his face.

"Now do ye Pharisees make clean the outside of the cup and the platter; but your inward part is full of ravening and wickedness." Ravening means grabbing, greed. It's a sharp thing to say at dinner, and Luke doesn't soften it. Then a question that turns it into a riddle: "did not he that made that which is without make that which is within also?" God made the cup's inside as well as its outside. You can't polish one and ignore the other. His answer to how is surprising: give alms from what's within, and everything is clean. Generosity cleans the inside of the cup. Then he names their careful tithing, a tenth of even mint and rue from the herb garden, and says they pass over justice and the love of God. But listen to how the sentence ends: "these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone." He doesn't throw out the small faithful habits. He says do both. This is the language of Israel's own prophets, who said the same thing to their own people. Micah asked what the Lord requires, and answered: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. Jewish teachers have said it ever since, and Christians have needed to hear it about their own churches just as often. This week has gathered round that question of inside and outside. Wisdom given to little ones. A Samaritan who stopped. Martha and Mary. A short prayer. A friend knocking at midnight. A lamp in the eye. And now a cup that needs washing on both sides.
screen: `DO BOTH: THE SMALL AND THE GREAT.`
then, large: `NOT TO LEAVE THE OTHER UNDONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clean something inside, not just outside. If there's a cup or a bowl near you, pick it up and look into it. If not, picture one. Then turn your attention inward. What's sitting inside you that nobody else can see? A grudge, a little greed, a story you tell yourself about someone. Don't scrub at it. Just name it honestly. Then think of one generous thing you could give today, from the inside out: time, money, a kind word you've been holding back. If you pray, you can offer that inside place to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
Clean on the outside. At a dinner table, Jesus says God made the inside of the cup too, and that generosity is what cleans it.
Your line: the inside too. Today, when you tidy a room or your face for someone, do one quiet, generous thing nobody will see. Day five hundred forty-six, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Many Christians pair outward practices, like grace before meals, tithing or fasting, with an inward examination of conscience, and churches often read this passage alongside the prophets in seasons of repentance such as Lent.

original.note: Greek: from within, the inside. the part of the cup, and of a person, that Jesus says God also made.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus was against religious rules.
what it means: he says the outward habits should be done, and the inside cleaned too, through justice, love of God and generosity.
what a scholar hears: he speaks as Israel's prophets did, from inside the tradition, as a guest at a Pharisee's table, not from outside it.

notes: Pharisees described as a devoted movement seeking holiness in daily life (meals, purity). Framed to avoid making them a foil; please check tone.
Luke 11:41 ('give alms of such things as ye have') is ambiguous in Greek ('the things within'); script paraphrases as 'give alms from what's within'. Confirm.
